title: Technical Analysis in Practice
summary: Use moving averages, momentum, volatility and volume with written rules, and test them honestly. Education only.

modules.title: Moving Averages and Trend
modules.subject: Trend indicators
modules.learned: Calculate a simple moving average and describe a trend from the slope and position of an average.

check.q: A trader wants to use a 20-period average to define the trend on a chart she trades. What should she write before she looks at the chart?
options: Only the broker's name and the lot size
A prediction of next month's price
The average length, the trend condition and the close that breaks the trend
Nothing, because averages are read after the trade
check.explanation: A trend rule written before the chart defines the average, the trend condition and what breaks it, so the reading can be tested.

modules.title: Momentum and the Relative Strength Index
modules.subject: Momentum
modules.learned: Explain what the relative strength index measures, read overbought and oversold labels with the trend, and identify divergence.

check.q: A relative strength reading is above 70 during a strong uptrend. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A certain fall within a few days
Strong recent gains, so the trend rule should decide the next step
The indicator is broken and should be removed
The trader should sell at once
check.explanation: The label describes momentum. The written rule, not the reading alone, decides what happens next.

modules.title: Volatility, True Range and ATR Stops
modules.subject: Volatility
modules.learned: Calculate true range and average true range, set a stop from ATR, and size the position for a fixed cash risk.

check.q: Overnight the ATR of a share rises from 1.2 to 2.0. A trader keeps a fixed 100 USD risk per trade. What should happen to the position size on a new trade?
options: It should rise, because volatility creates more opportunity
It should stay the same, because the chart looks familiar
It should fall, because the stop distance widens for the same cash risk
It should double to offset the higher volatility
check.explanation: A larger ATR widens the stop distance. Keeping the cash risk fixed means fewer units.

modules.title: Volume and Breakout Confirmation
modules.subject: Volume
modules.learned: Compare current volume with its average, judge a breakout against a written volume rule, and check the data source.

check.q: A breakout comes on relative volume of 0.7. What does the rule-based reading suggest?
options: Strong confirmation, so the trade should be doubled
Volume is irrelevant to this breakout
The breakout is certain to continue
Weak support, so the rule may say to skip or wait
check.explanation: Low relative volume is weak confirmation. The written rule decides whether that means skip, wait or reduce size.

modules.title: Combining Indicators and Timeframes
modules.subject: Alignment
modules.learned: Choose a small set of indicators with distinct roles, use a higher timeframe for context, and apply a yes-or-no checklist.

check.q: A trader's checklist requires the daily trend to be up and the four-hour timing condition to be met. What is the checklist's job?
options: To test whether every required condition is met before a trade happens
To predict the exact top of the move
To replace the stop order with a reminder
To count how many indicators the screen can show
check.explanation: A yes-or-no checklist makes the decision testable. A trade happens only when the required conditions are all yes.

modules.title: Backtesting Without Fooling Yourself
modules.subject: Backtesting
modules.learned: Describe what a backtest can and cannot show, split data into development and out-of-sample periods, and include realistic costs.

check.q: A rule looks excellent on the period used to design it but fails on new data. What is the most likely cause?
options: The new data is always wrong
Overfitting to the design period
The market has stopped moving
The trader used a stop, which always fails
check.explanation: A rule tuned to fit a period with many settings often fails on new data. That is overfitting, which is why out-of-sample tests exist.

questions.q: A trader's rule uses a 20-period average. Which average responds faster to a sudden price spike?
options: An exponential average, which gives recent closes more weight
A simple average, which weights every close equally
Neither, because both ignore recent closes
A 200-period average, because longer periods react faster

questions.q: Price has risen 6 percent from its low before a moving-average crossover appears. What does this show?
options: The crossover predicted the exact turn
The signal lags, so part of the move has already happened
The average is broken and should be removed
The signal confirms that the move will continue

questions.q: A five-period simple moving average uses closes of 20, 21, 22, 21 and 23. What is the average?
A rule breaks the trend after two closes below a rising 20-day average. Price closes below it on two consecutive days. What should the trader do?
options: Keep the trend, because averages are not reliable
Buy at once, because price is now cheap
Change the average to 50 days until the trend returns
Record the trend as broken and review the plan before any trade

questions.q: Why should a trader write down the averages and their lengths before reading a chart?
options: So the reading can be tested the same way every time
Because brokers require a written indicator list
Because averages change automatically over time
So the averages can be changed after a losing trade

questions.q: A relative strength reading rises above 70 during an uptrend that the rule already identified. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: The price must fall within a few sessions
The reading shows strong recent gains, so the trend rule should decide the next step
The indicator is broken and should be removed
The trader should double the position at once

questions.q: Which setup describes bullish divergence?
options: Price makes a higher high while the indicator makes a lower high, in an uptrend
Price and the indicator both make higher highs together
Price makes a lower low while the indicator makes a higher low, in a downtrend
Price stays flat while the indicator moves up sharply

questions.q: Who introduced the relative strength index, and in what year?
options: An exchange, in 1990
A financial regulator, in 2008
The index has no known author
J. Welles Wilder, in 1978

questions.q: What reading is commonly labelled overbought on a relative strength chart?
options: Above 70
Below 30
Exactly 50
Above 100

questions.q: A trader sees bearish divergence in an uptrend. Which response follows a written rule?
options: Sell everything, because divergence always ends the trend
Apply the size rule the plan sets for divergence, without assuming a fall
Ignore the rule, because divergence is never useful
Add to the position to profit from the reversal

questions.q: A session has a high of 52, a low of 49 and a previous close of 55. What is the true range?
Five true ranges of 1.2, 0.9, 1.5, 1.1 and 1.3 are averaged. What is the average true range?
An ATR of 1.2 and a multiple of 2 give a stop for a buy entry at 50.00. Where is the stop?
options: At 47.60, which is 2.4 below entry
At 48.80, which is 1.2 below entry
At 52.40, which is 2.4 above entry
At 49.40, which is 0.6 below entry

questions.q: Why does a higher ATR need a smaller position for the same cash risk?
options: A wider stop lowers the loss per unit, so more units fit
A wider stop raises the risk per unit, so fewer units fit the budget
Volatility always makes a trade unprofitable
ATR is a fixed number that never changes the size

questions.q: What does the average true range measure?
options: The direction of the trend
The expected profit of the next trade
How much price moves, not which direction it moves
The exact future price range

questions.q: A share breaks above a marked resistance level on volume of 0.6 times its average. What is the most careful reading?
options: The breakout is confirmed beyond doubt
Volume is irrelevant to any breakout
The level has moved, so the breakout is void
The breakout is weakly supported, and the rule may say to wait

questions.q: What does relative volume compare?
options: Current volume with its average over a chosen period
Today's price with yesterday's price
Volume on two different exchanges
The highest volume ever recorded

questions.q: What is tick volume?
options: The number of units traded on a regulated exchange
A count of price changes in a period, used where traded volume is not published
The total value of a position
A fee charged on each trade

questions.q: Why should relative volume be read at the close of a period?
options: Because brokers only publish closing volume
Because volume always falls before a close
Because partial volume changes the reading while the period is still forming
Because prices cannot be read during the day

questions.q: A breakout rule requires volume of at least 1.5 times its average. A breakout comes on 0.9 times. A friend says to buy anyway. What should the trader do?
options: Buy half now, because the rule is a formality
Buy at once, since the level is clearly broken
Change the threshold to 0.9 so the trade qualifies
Skip the trade and record the outcome to test whether the rule helps

questions.q: A daily chart shows a clear downtrend. A four-hour chart shows a short rise. Under a context-then-timing rule, what should the trader do?
options: Wait for a timing signal in the direction of the daily downtrend
Buy the short rise, since the lower timeframe is more recent
Ignore the daily chart because it is slower
Trade both directions at the same time

questions.q: Why is redundancy a problem in a set of indicators?
options: Repeated tools always cancel each other out
Repeated tools agree for the same reason and add no new information
Redundancy is required by regulators
Redundant tools measure different things

questions.q: What is the job of the higher timeframe in a context-then-timing rule?
options: To provide the exact entry price
To replace the stop order
To set the context and the direction of trades
To count the number of trades in a week

questions.q: What should a disagreement between timeframes lead to under a written rule?
options: Taking the trade on the lower timeframe
Trading the side with more indicators
Doubling the size to resolve the conflict
Waiting, unless the rule says otherwise

questions.q: A trader has eight indicators, four bullish and three bearish. What is the best next step?
options: Remove repeated indicators and apply the written checklist
Add a ninth indicator and follow the majority
Trade the side with the most indicators
Stop reading charts altogether

questions.q: What does a backtest show?
options: That the rule will work in future
How a written rule would have behaved on past data
The exact profit the trader will earn
The reliability of the broker

questions.q: A trader tests 40 versions of a rule and keeps the best. What is the main risk?
options: The best result is proven because it was the best
There is no risk, since each version was tested
The result is likely overfitted to one period
The broker will reject the rule

questions.q: What is the purpose of an out-of-sample period?
options: To choose the settings after seeing the results
To replace the development period entirely
To record the trader's emotions
To test a rule that was fixed before the test, on data not used to design it

questions.q: Which costs must a realistic backtest include?
options: Spread, commission and slippage on every simulated trade
Only the advertised commission
None, because backtests measure the rule only
Only the costs paid at the end of the year

questions.q: A rule is changed after it fails on the out-of-sample period, then retested on that same period. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The revised rule is now proven, because it passed
That period is used up, so the revised rule needs new data before it is trusted
The original test should be ignored and the new result accepted
The out-of-sample period was never needed
